aspects: What a tsunami is: a series of long waves from displaced water
Underwater earthquakes at subduction zones displacing the seafloor and water column
Other triggers: landslides, volcanic eruptions, and meteorite impacts displacing water
How tsunami waves travel across deep ocean: high speed, long wavelength, small height
Shoaling: wave slowing and growing taller as water becomes shallow near shore
Coastal destruction factors: inundation, repeated surges, backwash, coastline shape, and limits of warning

evaluation_claims.text: A tsunami is an immense wave generated when a large volume of water is displaced from its equilibrium position.
Most tsunamis are triggered by geologic activity along the Pacific Ocean's Ring of Fire, where tectonic plates collide and form deep ocean trenches.
Between 1900 and 2015, seventy-eight percent of confirmed tsunamis occurred in the Pacific Ocean.
Between 1900 and 2015, the highest share of Pacific tsunamis was generated off Japan and Indonesia.
Earthquakes along fault zones are the primary trigger of tsunamis.
Tsunamis can also be initiated by underwater submarine landslides, volcanic eruptions, above-water landslides, falling debris, or large atmospheric storms known as meteotsunamis.
Sediment movement, an explosive volcanic impulse, or falling mass displaces the water column, and gravity then propagates the disturbance outward across the sea.
In deep water, a tsunami moves at high speed with a very long wavelength, huge volumes of water, and a relatively small amplitude.
In deep water, the energy of a tsunami is primarily kinetic, stored in the rapid movement of the water.
Tsunamis become more destructive near the coast because of a process called shoaling.
As a tsunami enters shallower coastal areas, the wave begins to experience force from the seabed.
The shallower the water becomes, the slower the tsunami travels.
Because the front of the wave slows while the back continues moving forward, the waves bunch together and the wavelength decreases significantly.
Because a tsunami contains massive volumes of water within each wavelength, shortening the wavelength forces the amplitude to increase dramatically.
During shoaling, much of the wave's kinetic energy is converted into gravitational potential energy as water is pushed well above normal sea level.
When the stored potential energy reaches the shoreline, it causes massive inundation as water runs up onto and over the land.
During the 2004 Boxing Day tsunami, shoaling produced waves fifteen to thirty meters high that inundated coastlines.
The 2004 Boxing Day tsunami killed nearly a quarter of a million people.
A wave running up five to ten meters above normal sea level equals the height of a three-story building.
Earthquake-driven tsunamis can travel across entire ocean basins.
Tsunamis generated by non-seismic mechanisms such as submarine landslides tend to dissipate quickly and rarely affect distant coastlines.
Near their source, landslide-generated tsunamis can be larger than seismic tsunami waves and strike nearby coasts within minutes with little to no warning.

reference_verifications.rationale: Evidence says tsunamis result from water displaced from equilibrium position and large volume of water displaced, but no definition as 'immense wave'.
Directly stated.
78% of 754 confirmed tsunamis in Pacific between 1900 and 2015.
Highest percentages are off Japan (21%) and Indonesia (8%); the evidence frames it as share of all tsunamis since 1900, not strictly Pacific ones, a minor difference.
About 80% of tsunamis are triggered by earthquakes; usually caused by earthquakes along fault zones at plate boundaries.
Submarine landslides, volcanic eruptions, above-water landslides, falling debris and meteotsunamis from large storms are all mentioned.
Sediment movement alters sea level, gravity propagates; volcanic eruption impulsive force displaces water column; falling debris displaces water.
Deep water: very fast, long wavelength, small amplitude, large volumes of water.
Evidence says energy is mostly kinetic when propagating across the ocean; 'primarily' matches 'mostly'.
Shoaling is described as one reason tsunamis cause so much damage near coasts, with wave height growing.
Shoaling happens because waves experience force from the seabed as water gets shallower.
Directly states the shallower the water, the slower the wave.

Evidence says waves slow and bunch together, shortening wavelength; the front-slows/back-continues mechanism is implied (trailing waves faster) but not explicitly stated, and 'significantly' is only loosely supported.
States tsunamis involve large volumes of water in each wavelength, so wavelength can decrease by a large proportion and amplitude increase by a lot.
Says a lot of kinetic energy is converted to potential energy due to gravity as water is much higher than normal level.
Evidence says stored energy is unleashed when it runs up onto and over the land; inundation is linked to shoaling.
Evidence states waves 15–30m high in 2004 Boxing Day tsunami, in a shoaling context; 'inundated coastlines' is a mild inference.
Evidence says nearly a quarter of a million killed.
Evidence says up to 10 m is about a 3-storey building height; the 5–10 m range equaling that is stronger than stated.
Evidence says tsunamis, usually earthquake-caused, can travel across entire ocean basins.
Pacific Tsunami Museum says non-seismic tsunamis usually dissipate quickly and rarely affect far coastlines; NOAA says the same of landslide tsunamis.
NOAA directly states landslide tsunamis may be larger near source and impact coasts within minutes with little to no warning.

citation_entailment_verifications.rationale: Evidence says falling debris displaces water from equilibrium position and produces a tsunami, but doesn't define a tsunami as an 'immense wave' from a large volume of water.
Directly stated: most tsunamis triggered by Ring of Fire activity; plates collide forming deep ocean trenches.
78% of 754 confirmed tsunamis 1900-2015 were in the Pacific.
Evidence says highest percentages since 1900 are off Japan (21%) and Indonesia (8%), but it's not specifically a share of Pacific tsunamis and the period is 'since 1900'.

Evidence says trenches are often the source of earthquakes that trigger tsunamis and that most tsunami-causing landslides are earthquake-caused, but doesn't explicitly state earthquakes are the primary trigger.
Submarine landslides, volcanic eruptions, above-water landslides, falling debris, and storm-caused meteotsunamis are all covered across the passages.
Sediment movement, volcanic impulsive force, and falling debris displace water; gravitational forces propagate the tsunami.
Fast speed, long wavelength, small amplitude, and large water volumes are supported, but 'huge volumes' is a paraphrase of 'large volumes'. Mostly supported.
Evidence says the energy is mostly kinetic (movement) energy in the ocean, but doesn't say 'primarily stored in rapid movement'; this is a minor paraphrase.
Shoaling is described as one reason tsunamis cause so much damage to coastal areas; 'because of' is slightly stronger than 'one reason'.
Evidence says shoaling happens because waves experience force from the seabed as water gets shallower.
States 'the shallower the water, the slower the wave'.
Evidence says waves slow, bunch together, and wavelength decreases (by a large proportion). It does not mention the front slowing while the back continues moving forward.
Evidence says tsunamis involve large volumes of water per wavelength, so wavelength decrease allows amplitude to increase by a lot.
Evidence says a lot of kinetic energy is converted to potential energy because water is much higher than normal level, due to gravity.
Energy stored is unleashed when it runs up onto and over the land; shoaling causes inundation. 'Massive' is slight embellishment.
Evidence says waves 15–30m high in 2004 tsunami, but doesn't explicitly attribute to shoaling in that statement or say inundated coastlines; shoaling is discussed generally.
States it killed nearly a quarter of a million people in total.
Evidence says up to 10 m is about a 3-storey building; 5–10 m wave is mentioned, but equating 5–10 m to 3 storeys is not stated (only 10 m).
Mentions 'ocean-wide tsunamis caused by some earthquakes', implying basin-wide travel, and contrasts with non-seismic ones; not explicit about crossing basins.

E-76748bba4f5f says non-seismic tsunamis usually dissipate quickly and rarely affect distant coastlines; E-ecbf878fe71b says landslide tsunamis lose energy quickly and rarely affect distant coastlines.
E-ecbf878fe71b states landslide-generated tsunamis may be larger than seismic tsunamis near their source and can impact coastlines within minutes with little to no warning.

additional_metric_details.notes: All scores are Claude judgments, not verified ground truth. Repair effectiveness compares coverage/narration, not factual truth. No revision or no retrieval is N/A rather than zero.

metric_semantics.reference_evidence_support_percent: Evidence entailment within the frozen reference corpus; not factual accuracy.
metric_semantics.query_coverage_percent: Coverage of a fixed six-aspect checklist derived once per question from the question text and shared by all systems; missing/duplicate judge outputs are normalized against that fixed denominator.
metric_semantics.narration_input: Coverage, relevance, narration and grounded-requirement judgements use the complete script with [E-...] evidence markers removed; claim extraction and citation metrics use the marked script. Aspect scores are continuous in [0, 1].
metric_semantics.narration_quality_percent: Ten-dimension spoken educational narration score; excludes factual truth.
metric_semantics.citation_precision: Share of emitted citation IDs that are identified as supporting the claim when verification is restricted to cited passages.
metric_semantics.citation_recall: Share of all citation-required extracted factual claims that have at least one cited passage judged to support the claim.
metric_semantics.evaluation_estimated_llm_cost_usd: Evaluator telemetry. CLI mode uses Claude Code's reported list-price equivalent; API mode uses the configured Anthropic per-token rates.
